title: Two faces of symmetry match in gear-like coupled rotary motors
abstract: Rotary molecular motors commonly couple components with different rotational symmetries, but how this gearing controls energy transduction remains unclear. Here we show that symmetry can produce a fundamental tradeoff in coupled stochastic barrierless rotary motors: the gear ratio that maximizes output power under tight coupling is also the ratio that requires the strongest coupling to remain locked. Consequently, weakening the coupling can invert the effect of gearing, transforming a power maximum into a local minimum. At strong driving, both the power-optimal and most slip-susceptible ratios approach symmetry match. Numerical solutions of the Fokker-Planck dynamics for rotors with finite energy barriers reproduce these predictions and reveal how the behavior changes when driving strength is fixed per rotation or per subunit. Motivated by the bacterial flagellar motor, these results identify coupling strength as a key determinant of whether matched rotational symmetries enhance or suppress energy transduction, providing a general design principle for coupled molecular motors.
summary: This work analyzes coupled rotary motors, modeling them as gear-like systems whose energy transduction efficiency depends critically on symmetry matching. The authors find that while strong coupling favors symmetry matching for maximum power, weakening this coupling can destabilize the system, causing the optimal ratio to shift dramatically. This offers a general design principle for understanding how molecular motors operate.
main_problem: The paper investigates how symmetry matching in gear-like coupled rotary motors controls the efficiency of energy transduction.
main_result: The optimal gear ratio for maximum power under strong coupling approaches symmetry match, but weakening the coupling can invert this effect, turning the power maximum into a local minimum.
method: The study uses numerical solutions of the Fokker-Planck dynamics and analytical derivations for the barrierless limit to model the coupled rotors.
model_or_system: The system models two coupled rotary molecular motors (like the C-ring–MS-ring in bacterial flagella) diffusing on periodic energy landscapes defined by a coupled potential. The dynamics are governed by the Fokker-Planck equation.
key_observables: Output power ($P_1$) as a function of the upstream rotor's subunit number ($n_o$), and the coupling strength ($E_c$).
important_parameters: Coupling strength ($E_c$), driving forces ($\mu_o, \mu_1$), and the ratio of subunit numbers ($n_o/n_1$).
main_assumptions: The analysis compares results from the full Fokker-Planck dynamics (with finite barriers) against simplified barrierless models and Langevin descriptions.
figures_summary: Figures illustrate schematics of the BFM structure and gear-like coupling, showing output power vs. subunit number for various coupling strengths and driving schemes.
paper_structure: The paper progresses by defining the physical model and Hamiltonian, analyzing the dynamics in different coupling regimes (tight, intermediate, weak), deriving analytical results for the barrierless limit, and finally comparing these predictions with full numerical simulations.
why_interesting: The study provides a general design principle for coupled molecular motors, showing how symmetry constraints dictate energy transduction efficiency, which is relevant to non-equilibrium statistical mechanics in biological systems.

figures.caption: FIG. 1. Schematics of Salmonella’s flagellar motor structure. a) The BFM consists of multiple rings: the C-ring, MS-ring, P-ring, and L-ring. A stator (composed of MotA and MotB proteins) binds to the peptidoglycan (PG) layer and rotates driven by ion flow. Rotation of the stators rotates the C-ring, which rotates the MS-ring, which in turn rotates the rod and the hook, and hence the flagellum. The motor is embedded in multiple layers: outer membrane (OM), PG, and cytoplasmic membrane (CM). b) When stators (light green) interact with the C-ring (purple), they drive the ring to rotate. c) Rotation of the C-ring drives rotation of the MS-ring (blue) in the same direction.

FIG. 2. a) Schematic of gear-like coupling between arbi- trary rotors Ro (blue) and R1 (red). The number of teeth on each gear corresponds to the number n of subunits. µo and µ1 represent the respective driving forces (constant or scaling) on Ro and R1. b, c) Schematic of a possible tra- jectory contributing to slippage under intermediate-strength gear-like coupling. When one tooth from each rotor (here, dark blue and dark red) come in contact (b), the upstream rotor (Ro) can capitalize on the flexible coupling and rotate 2π/no while R1 maintains the same orientation (c).

FIG. 3. Output power βP1 as a function of the number no of Ro subunits, for different coupling strengths βEc under constant driving. Rows each have fixed driving force βµo on Ro ranging from 8 to 64; columns each have fixed number n1 of R1 subunits ranging from 3 to 7. Gray vertical solid lines: symmetry match (n1 = no). Blue dashed vertical lines: power-maximizing n∗o predicted by finite-barrier tight-coupling theory (S23). βµ1 = −2 and βEo = βE1 = 2 throughout. Here and throughout other figures, shared axes use the same scales, and curves connecting data points are included as guides to the eye.

FIG. 4. Occurrence of output-power global maxima and local minima under constant driving, as functions of the driving-force ratio −µo/µ1 and coupling strength βEc, for n1 = 3,5, and 7. For each parameter combination, blue and red circles indicate the presence of an interior global maximum or local minimum, respectively, in P1 as a function of upstream symmetry no. Extrema at the boundaries (no = 1,30) are excluded. Black dashed lines show the deterministic barrierless locking threshold (7) evaluated at no = n1. βµ1 = −2 and βEo = βE1 = 2 throughout.

FIG. 5. Output power under scaling driving, as a function of the number no of Ro subunits, for different coupling strengths βEc. Each row has a fixed per-subunit driving force βµsub o on Ro (1 on the top row and 8 on the bottom); each column has fixed number n1 of subunits of R1 ranging from 3 to 7. Gray vertical solid lines show symmetry match (n1 = no). βµsub 1 = −2/3 and βEo = βE1 = 2 throughout.
